bib.title: Cost-Effective, Low Latency Vector Search with Azure Cosmos DB

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Cost-Effective, Low Latency Vector Search with Azure Cosmos DB", first author Nitish Upreti (plus Simhadri, Krishnaswamy and about 30 other Microsoft authors). Venue: PVLDB 18(12): 5166-5183, 2025 (doi 10.14778/3750601.3750635), arXiv 2505.05885. Peer-reviewed, not a preprint.

COVERAGE: All 18 pages, 94,390 chars. I read the body, evaluation, related work, conclusion and all appendices (A-F) in full. I skimmed the reference list (about lines 296-495 of my filtered copy) for origins only. I filtered out numeric-only plot-axis lines in the extraction. I did not run the figure-caption script and took captions from the text. Page numbers are not in the extraction, so locations are given as sections.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Vector index inside an operational DB: one DiskANN index per partition, stored as Bw-Tree index terms (quantized vectors plus adjacency lists), updated on every insert with no segment merge or rebuild.
  number: none
  setup: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, DiskANN rewritten in Rust, partition limit 50 GB
  quote: "Instead, for simplicity and robustness of the system, we store the terms representing the vector index on the Bw-Tree index in Cosmos DB." and "A vector insert results in immediate and durable changes to the index terms to Bw-Tree, and does not require further indexing or merging down the line."
  where: Sec 1
- Query cost is far lower than serverless vector DBs.
  number: 70 RU/query, $17.50 per 1M queries vs Pinecone $768, Zilliz $220, DataStax $30.72
  setup: 10M Wiki-Cohere 768-dim vectors, recall@10 94.64%, serverless enterprise tiers, public pricing as of 14 Jul 2025; Cosmos cost from own tests at default settings
  quote: "Cosmos DB has nearly 43×, 12×, and 1.75× lower query cost than Pinecone (enterprise tier), Zilliz (enterprise tier), and DataStax (standard tier) respectively."
  where: Sec 4.1, Table 1
- Latency: p50 under 20 ms at 10M vectors.
  number: 91.83% recall@10 at LSearch=50 (the Fig 6 legend says 91.43; text and figure disagree)
  setup: 10M Wiki-Cohere, 768-dim, client fetches the underlying docs, 5000 queries one at a time, warm Bw-Tree cache
  quote: "with LSearch=50, p50 latency is under 20 ms for the 10 million index with a recall@10 of 91.83%."
  where: Sec 4.1, Fig 6
- Latency and cost scale sub-linearly with index size and are insensitive to dimension.
  number: under 2x for 100x growth
  setup: 100K to 10M vectors, L=100; Wiki-Cohere 768-dim and MSTuring 100-dim
  quote: "the p50, p95 and p99 latencies increase by less than 2× despite the 100× increase in index size." and "despite the increase in dimensionality from 100 to 768, there is barely any increase in query latency or cost"
  where: Sec 4.1, Figs 7-8. Wiki-Cohere 10M RU is the exception because it ran on 2 partitions.
- In-place delete keeps recall stable under updates.
  number: +1-3 points on expiration runbooks, up to 20 points on the clustered runbook
  setup: runbooks on WikiCohere-10M, MSTuring-1M and MSTuring-10M (32 clusters, distribution shift); R=32, Lbuild=100, Lsearch=200; compared with a "drop" baseline
  quote: "in-place deletes achieve recall that is as much as 20 percentage points higher than the baseline"
  where: Sec 4.5, Fig 13
- Filter-aware search (beta-biased greedy search) gives better tail latency and cost than post-filtering.
  number: 10x better p99 latency, 5x less p99 cost at L=200
  setup: YFCC 1M, 192-dim CLIP vectors with metadata; beta=0.3. Filter-aware recall is 98.60 vs post-filter 99.92 at L=200.
  quote: "L = 200 with filter-aware search yields the similar recall as L = 200 with post-filtering search, but with 10x better p99 latency and 5x less p99 cost."
  where: Sec 4.2, Fig 9. Filters matching fewer than 5000 docs go to a flat or quantized scan instead.
- Sharded (per-tenant) index beats one global index with a filter.
  number: 98.09% recall@10 at p99 13.43 ms, vs 66.17% at p99 38.59 ms (Ls=100) and 87% at p99 164 ms (Ls=1000)
  setup: YFCC, year as shard key
  quote: "Sharded (Ls = 100) 7.28 10.07 13.43 98.09 / Non-Sharded (Ls = 100) 22.40 21.29 38.59 66.17"
  where: Table 3, Sec 4.6
- Scale-out to a billion vectors. Recall at the tested L values is modest.
  number: 1B across 50 partitions; recall@10 about 83.8/89.6/93.9 at L=50/100/200
  setup: MSTuring 1B and 100M, 100-dim, client on an E64is_v3 VM with 64 vCPUs. Which recall line belongs to 1B vs 100M is ambiguous in the extraction.
  quote: "The MS Turing 1 billion vector collection spans 50 partitions, while the 100 million vector collection spans 20."
  where: Sec 4.3, Fig 10. Cost grows "logarithmically with the number of vectors in a partition, but linearly with the number of partitions."
- Ingest rate and cost.
  number: about 25 ms CPU per insert, 40 vectors/s per thread, 640/s on 16 cores; 65 RU/insert, $162.5 per 10M vectors
  setup: R=32, Lbuild=100, 16 physical / 32 vCPU machine, Resource Governance disabled for the measurement; WikiCohere-10M; July 2025 prices
  quote: "This yields a throughput of 40 vectors/sec per thread, or 640 vectors/sec on a 16-core machine"
  where: Sec 4.4, Table 2. Cheaper than Pinecone ($240) and DataStax ($307.2), but "5.4× higher insertion charges than Zilliz" ($30). Autoscale/provisioned billing gives "at least a 7× price discount".
- Quantization lets the index navigate in cache and touch few full vectors.
  number: about 3500 quantized vs about 50 full-precision vectors per query; PQ 96x compression of text-3-large (12 KB); 128 B PQ to navigate, 256 B to prune
  setup: top-10, degree 32, L=100; OpenAI text-3-large embeddings
  quote: "a query for top-10 entries on a graph with degree 32 and search list size L = 100 might touch about 3500 quantized vectors, but only about 50 full precision vectors."
  where: Sec 3.2, Sec 2.1. PQ is built from about 1000 samples, re-quantized at 25,000 samples with no graph rebuild.
- Segment-based vector indexes (SingleStore, Elastic) are criticised.
  number: none
  quote: "(a) each query has to fan out to numerous segments which limits query efficiency, (b) regular rebuilds of vector indices are needed as segments are merged or consolidated, which consumes significant compute, memory and causes serious latency spikes"
  where: Sec 1
- DiskANN I/O and memory background (cited from earlier work, not measured here).
  number: 90% recall@10 on billion-scale SIFT with 50 random 4 KB SSD reads
  quote: "it can achieve 90% recall@10 on a billion-size SIFT dataset with just 50 random 4 KB reads to SSD."
  where: Sec 2.1
- Memory comparison with SingleStore-V and Elastic.
  number: under 5 GB memory for 10M-vector indexes over 12 KB embeddings
  setup: authors' claim; SingleStore used a 256 GB / 32-core machine for its 10M experiments
  quote: "we use <5GB of memory even for 10 million scale indices over 12 KB embeddings."
  where: Sec 5.2
- Cost vs DataStax and Elastic.
  number: Cosmos autoscale under $50/month vs DataStax $900/month (10 QPS, 1M index); Elastic about $500/month (15 GB DRAM machine) vs Cosmos about $30 at 500 RU/s (10 QPS) or $300 at 5000 RU/s (100 QPS)
  quote: "A manually provisioned Cosmos DB service for 500 RU/sec or 5000 RU/sec would serve 10 QPS and 100 QPS and cost about $30 and $300/month respectively."
  where: Sec 5.2
- Graph vs partition indexes: query complexity grows logarithmically for graphs and faster for IVF/LSH.
  number: none
  quote: "Partition-based algorithms benefit from shorter indexing times than graph algorithms on average, but their query complexity increases much faster with the size of the dataset"
  where: Sec 5.1, Fig 14

LIMITS
- Vendor paper. The authors built and benchmarked their own product, and the cost comparison uses public price lists, not measured competitor runs. It is dated 14 Jul 2025 and prices will have dated.
- Cosmos cost comes from RUs, while rivals use Read Units and vCUs, so the units are not directly comparable. The 43x and 12x figures depend on serverless pricing. Provisioned or autoscale Cosmos is cheaper still.
- No head-to-head latency or recall runs against Pinecone, Zilliz or DataStax. pgvector and pgvectorscale are explicitly not benchmarked: "We leave an exhaustive benchmarking against these systems for future work."
- Recall at 1B is under 94% at L=200. Best end-to-end latency needs few, packed partitions.
- Vectors are limited to one per path. The 50 GB partition cap and 5 s backend request limit force continuations. Vector search continuations are not streaming, so the client re-orders and merges partial results.
- Insert throughput measured with Resource Governance off. Graph updates run outside the transaction path and are rate-limited.
- Quantized data should "more natural[ly]" use the forward term type, which the authors say they will reconcile later.
- Memory claims assume a Bw-Tree cache large enough for quantized and adjacency terms.

BUILDS ON: DiskANN (Subramanya et al., NeurIPS 2019, as cited [38]); FreshDiskANN [36]/in-place delete [44]; ParlayANN [25] for mini-batch; Filtered-DiskANN [16]; Bw-Tree latch-free index and the Cosmos DB system paper [32]; product quantization (Jegou et al. [19]). Comparisons: SingleStore-V (PVLDB 2024), Elastic, JVector, pgvector, pgvectorscale, V-Base, AnalyticDB-V, Turbopuffer.

CODE
- Query syntax (Sec 3.5): `SELECT TOP 10 c.title FROM c WHERE c.category = 'category1' ORDER BY VectorDistance(c.embedding, [..], false, {'searchListSizeMultiplier':10, 'quantizedVectorListMultiplier':7})`. The third argument is true for exact search.
- Pseudocode: Algorithm 1 GreedySearch, Algorithm 3 RobustPrune, Algorithm 7 BetaSearch (scales distance by beta<1 when the label matches).

FIGURES (captions from the text; page numbers unavailable)
- Fig 2: storage media for monolithic DiskANN-on-SSD vs the new stateless DiskANN over Cosmos index structures. Shows the decoupled layout.
- Fig 4: index term layout for quantized vectors and adjacency lists.
- Fig 5: re-ranking 10 neighbours from quantized space to get top-4 (quantizedVectorListMultiplier=2.5).
- Fig 6: p50/p95/p99 latency and RU for the 10M Wiki-Cohere index across search list sizes, with recall.
- Fig 9: post-filter vs filter-aware search on YFCC.
- Fig 10: 1B and 100M MSTuring latency and RU.
- Fig 13: recall over update runbooks, Drop vs In-place Delete.
- Fig 14: distance comparisons vs recall@5 for DiskANN, clustering and cross-polytope LSH.

FIT TO NOTES
- grep DiskANN gives 0 matches in both 04-vector-databases-and-ann.md and 09-vector-database-comparison.md. The notes do not say any of this.
- Strongest bearing is on "The other index families" in 04 (table of LSH/HNSW/IVF/PQ/Annoy at about line 206). It has no disk-resident graph index (DiskANN/Vamana), and no quantized-traversal-then-rerank pattern, which is the PQ-in-graph point (Sec 3.2, 5.1). It also bears on "What a vector database adds" (about line 261), which lists CRUD, filtering and persistence. The paper adds evidence that delete handling matters (+20 points of recall on a distribution-shift runbook), that filtered search is a distinct problem (filter-aware vs post-filter), and that per-tenant sharding beats a global filter.
- In 09 it bears on the pgvector section (pgvectorscale uses DiskANN) and on "Pitfalls"/"Migration notes", for the sync and duplication argument.
- It would be a "sharpens" or new citation for the "HNSW is memory-hungry" point, not a new core claim.

PROBLEMS: Extraction is clean text. Plot data and legends are interleaved in places, and the Fig 6 legend labels "L Search=20" are probably 200. Fig 6 recall for L=50 differs between text (91.83) and legend (91.43). The Fig 10 recall assignment is ambiguous. No embedded instructions found.
